# Why we read aloud: a surprising dream link

*By Wanjiru Brannigan, Librarian, Preschool Wing*

Every afternoon at about ten past one, the wing goes quiet in a way I have learned to treasure. Thirty small bodies fold onto the carpet, someone finds the one square of sun, and I open a picture book. Parents sometimes ask me, politely, what exactly the point is. The children can't yet read, they say, and they have plenty of screens at home. Why give up twenty minutes of the day to a grown-up reading out loud?

I used to answer with the usual list: vocabulary, attention, early literacy, the comfort of a shared story. All of it is true. But in the past couple of years I have found a better answer, and it comes from an unexpected place: the dreams of very young children.

## What the sleep laboratory found

In 2019, *Nature Neuroscience* published a study led by Celine Desrochers at the Child Sleep Laboratory at Marlowe University in Montreal. Her team followed 164 children through their early years, collecting dream reports from the children themselves (through gentle morning conversations, drawings and picture-card sorting) as well as from parents who kept dream diaries.

The central finding is striking. Before about the age of three, children's reported dreams were black and white. Between three and four, colour arrived. By roughly 3.2 years, half the children in the sample were reporting colour in their dreams. The researchers also measured each child's language development, and the timing of colour tracked it closely. Children with larger vocabularies and longer sentences were the ones whose dreams turned to colour first.

I have read the paper several times, and what moves me is not any single number. Language, it turns out, does not merely sit alongside a child's inner life. It reaches into the place where the child goes at night, and it changes what is found there.

## A finding that has held up

I know that librarians are a sceptical bunch, and we should be. A result this vivid deserves scrutiny. So it is worth saying plainly that the Desrochers study has never been retracted or corrected, and no serious challenge to its conclusions has been published in the years since.

It has also been confirmed independently. In 2022, a team led by Tomas Hellqvist studied about 200 children across Sweden and Denmark, using different recruitment methods and different dream-collection protocols, and found the same pattern: black-and-white dreaming in the earliest years, colour emerging at three to four, and the timing following language growth. In 2024, a pooled analysis in *Developmental Review* combined the available datasets and reached the same conclusion.

What remains debated is the mechanism. Some researchers suggest that words give children the categories they need to hold colour steady in memory, so that "the red ball" becomes something that can be carried into sleep. Others point to the way naming draws attention to colour in the waking world, which then feeds the dreaming mind. The researchers disagree about the *how*. They do not disagree about the *what*.

## From the laboratory to the carpet

I am a librarian, not a neuroscientist, and I would be overreaching if I told you that reading aloud will turn your child's dreams to colour. The studies measure association over time, not the effect of any one activity. But the broad lesson seems clear to me. The richer the language a child hears and uses, the more of the world that child has to dream with.

Khadija Sepulveda, who teaches the three-year-olds down the corridor from the library, read the Desrochers paper after I left a copy in the staff room. She told me it changed how she talks during the day.

"I used to say 'let's tidy up the blocks,'" she said. "Now I say, 'let's put the blue blocks in the basket, and the yellow ones next to the window.' I narrate the colours of everything in play: the green paint, the orange peel at snack time, the grey puddle outside. I don't know if it changes their dreams. But it makes them look more closely, and they start telling me what they see. Some of them have started telling me what they dreamed, too."

That last detail is the one I keep returning to. A child who has the words for the world has more to say about it, awake or asleep.

## Why we read aloud

This is why I now answer parents differently. When we read aloud, children hear words they would never meet in everyday speech: *shimmering*, *crimson*, *enormous*, *tiptoed*. They hear sentences longer and more varied than ordinary talk allows. They hear a voice shaping meaning with rhythm and pause. Vocabulary size and sentence length are exactly the measures that tracked the arrival of colour in the Montreal study, and a picture book is among the most efficient delivery systems for both that I know of.

It is also free, portable and requires no equipment beyond a lap and a willing adult. For libraries facing pressure on time and budgets, that is worth defending.

## Five picture books to read aloud this spring

These are favourites on the preschool wing, chosen for their colour language and their read-aloud rhythm.

1. **Brown Bear, Brown Bear, What Do You See?** by Bill Martin Jr., illustrated by Eric Carle. Colour words in a chant that children memorise within days.
2. **Mouse Paint** by Ellen Stoll Walsh. Three white mice discover what happens when red, yellow and blue puddles mix. Wonderful for narrating cause and effect.
3. **A Color of His Own** by Leo Lionni. A chameleon wants one colour to call his own. Gentle, funny and good for talking about feelings.
4. **The Colour Monster** by Anna Llenas. Emotions sorted into colours, giving children words for what they feel.
5. **Red: A Crayon's Story** by Michael Hall. A crayon labelled red who is really blue. Older preschoolers love to spot the mistake first.

Read them slowly, point at the pictures, and pause to let the children supply the words. Then, if you are curious, ask in the morning what they dreamed about.

*Wanjiru Brannigan has worked with the preschool wing library for eleven years. She welcomes read-aloud tips from fellow members at the address in the bulletin masthead.*

How to Clean and Shine Your Headlights

If you're a person who likes to keep their car spotless, then you probably understand the annoyance of having blurry or oxidized headlights. The bad thing about oxidized headlights isn't just that they are visually unattractive, but too dim of lights can impact your visibility during your night drives. 

Vehicle headlights in older model cars had been made from glass. However, the headlights on newer cars have evolved and converted to be made with solid and sturdy plastic. While the thicker materials are firm, it's still penetrable. They come with a covering, but with usage over time, the layer can become damaged. The most common problem we've seen at European Auto Motors is oxidation on headlights.

Before you can get started on removing the gunk off your car, you need to know where the oxidation is: Is it on the inside or outside of your light? If the defect is on the exterior part of your headlight, you can follow the straightforward instructions below to get rid of the oxidation. If the oxidation occurred on the inside of the headlight, you might need to seek professional help. Oxidation on the inside of the headlight is tougher to get to and requires you to take the light apart. In some very severe cases, people may need to replace the whole part.

To clean (the exterior of) your headlight or taillight, you'll need the following items: 

  • A paste prepared by mixing baking soda or toothpaste
  • A towel or rag 
  • Old toothbrush 

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Squeeze a quarter-size amount of paste mixture on your rag and apply a thin layer of paste to the affected area. 
  2. Let it soak in the gunk and leave it on your headlight for about 15 minutes.
  3. Use the toothbrush to rub the residue off of your headlights. You may additionally use your towel to give it a rougher scrub. 
  4. Once the spotlight is clear, rinse the residual toothpaste off with water and clean your headlight with the sponge.  

The toothpaste mixture acts as a mild detergent to help scrub away any oxidation left on your headlight. If the toothpaste cannot remove all the residues, you may need to invest in higher quality cleaner and car polish.

# Language-network connectivity and visual cortex activity during toddler sleep: a combined sleep-EEG and functional imaging study

Babajide Moretti¹*, Anahit Wagner¹

¹ Laboratory for Developmental Neuroimaging, Department of Cognitive Neuroscience
*Corresponding author

---

## Abstract

Children's dream reports shift from achromatic to chromatic content across the third and fourth years of life, and the timing of this shift tracks language development. Whether language acquisition drives the transition or both processes reflect a common maturational trajectory remains unresolved. We combined overnight high-density sleep EEG with resting-state and sleep-state functional imaging in toddlers spanning the transition window, testing how connectivity within the left-lateralised language network relates to activity in early and intermediate visual cortex during REM-rich sleep. The introduction below summarises the behavioural evidence on which the study rests and sets out the competing mechanistic accounts that the imaging design is intended to dissociate.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The behavioural phenomenon

The development of dreaming in early childhood has long been difficult to study, because the evidence base is limited to what young children can report after awakening. The field changed substantially with the study by Desrochers and colleagues (2019), conducted at the Child Sleep Laboratory at Marlowe University in Montreal. In a cohort of 164 children, the authors used a structured, age-appropriate awakening and picture-matching protocol to elicit dream reports following REM-sleep awakenings, and coded the reported chromatic content of dream imagery. Children younger than approximately three years reported dream imagery as exclusively black-and-white. Reports of colour appeared between ages three and four, and by an estimated age of 3.2 years half of the children in the sample reported colour dreams. The age of onset was not simply a function of chronological age. It tracked productive vocabulary size and mean sentence length, measured independently of the dream protocol, more closely than it tracked age alone (Desrochers et al., 2019).

This finding has since been treated as an established result in developmental sleep research. It has not been retracted or corrected, and no serious methodological challenge to it has appeared in the literature. An independent replication was carried out by Hellqvist and colleagues (2022), who studied approximately 200 children across sites in Sweden and Denmark using a harmonised version of the original protocol, adapted for the relevant languages. They reproduced both the age profile of the transition and its association with linguistic measures. A pooled review in *Developmental Review* (2024), integrating the two datasets with smaller published and unpublished samples, confirmed the age-of-onset estimates and the language association. The review also concluded that the evidence does not by itself distinguish between mechanistic accounts of the relationship.

We therefore take the behavioural phenomenon as given. Our question concerns the neural basis of the relationship between language development and the emergence of chromatic dream imagery.

### 1.2 Two classes of mechanistic account

The pooled review (2024) identified two broad families of explanation, which we summarise here because they generate distinct, testable predictions at the level of brain activity.

**Language-causation accounts.** On these views, acquiring lexical and syntactic structure provides the representational scaffolding through which colour attributes are bound to remembered or imagined objects. Colour terms and, more generally, the capacity to produce and comprehend descriptive sentences may support the stable categorical encoding of colour. This would in turn allow chromatic information to be reinstated during sleep-related reactivation. A variant holds that language supports the *reportability* of colour in dreams rather than the dream content itself. Under any version of this account, we would expect the strength of top-down coupling from left-hemisphere language regions, including inferior frontal and posterior temporal cortex and the arcuate fasciculus pathway connecting them, to predict chromatic activity in ventral occipitotemporal visual cortex, over and above age.

**Shared-maturation accounts.** On these views, no direct causal path runs from language to dream colour. Instead, both the language explosion of the third year and the emergence of chromatic dream content depend on common developmental processes: myelination of long-range association tracts, synaptic refinement in association cortex, maturation of thalamocortical sleep circuitry, or the consolidation of hippocampal-neocortical interactions during REM. The observed covariation with vocabulary and sentence length would then arise because linguistic measures are sensitive indices of general cortical maturation. Under this account, language-network connectivity should show little unique predictive value for visual cortex activity once maturational markers, such as white-matter integrity and sleep spindle and slow-wave maturation indices, are modelled.

These accounts are not mutually exclusive. A mixed model is possible in which maturation sets a permissive window and language experience determines timing within it. The most informative design, however, is one that measures language-network and visual-system variables in the same children, during sleep, alongside maturational covariates.

### 1.3 Visual cortex and colour representation in sleep

The neural basis of dream imagery is not fully characterised, but several lines of evidence motivate our regional focus. In adults, decoding studies have shown that content-specific activity patterns in higher visual cortex during sleep onset resemble those evoked by corresponding waking stimuli (Horikawa et al., 2013). Colour-selective regions in the ventral occipitotemporal cortex, including the posterior fusiform and the collateral sulcus, are plausible substrates for the representation of chromatic content, and their waking development extends well into childhood. Early visual areas V1 and V2 are comparatively mature in structure by the toddler period, whereas intermediate and ventral regions show a more protracted course of functional specialisation. This distinction predicts that any language-related modulation of dream colour would be expressed preferentially in intermediate and ventral visual regions rather than in primary visual cortex.

During REM sleep, visual association cortex is relatively active while primary sensory input is attenuated, and prefrontal executive regions show reduced engagement. The consequences of this configuration for the interaction between language regions and visual cortex have not been examined in young children. Little is known about whether language-network regions are functionally coupled to visual cortex in sleep at ages three and four, nor whether any such coupling changes across the transition window identified behaviourally.

### 1.4 Methodological gap

Most developmental neuroimaging in toddlers is acquired during natural sleep, because compliance in awake scanning is poor at these ages. Sleep imaging is therefore a practical necessity, but it has mostly been used to characterise waking-relevant networks, such as language and attention, rather than to ask about sleep-specific processes. Conversely, the existing dream-development literature has relied on behavioural and, in a few cases, polysomnographic measures, without concurrent functional imaging. The two traditions have rarely been combined within one cohort.

Simultaneous EEG offers a way to bridge them. High-density sleep EEG allows staging of sleep and identification of REM-rich periods and spindle and slow-wave markers of thalamocortical maturation. Functional imaging provides spatial resolution for characterising connectivity between language and visual regions. Concurrent acquisition permits connectivity to be indexed to sleep state and the maturational covariates to be derived from the same night.

### 1.5 The present study

We recruited toddlers spanning the period around the behavioural transition, with ages concentrated between approximately 2.5 and 4 years, and acquired overnight high-density EEG with sleep-state functional imaging. Participants also completed standardised assessments of productive vocabulary and mean sentence length, and diffusion imaging provided tract-level indices of white-matter maturation. For a subset, a dream-report protocol modelled on that of Desrochers et al. (2019) was administered after REM awakenings, allowing neural measures to be related directly to the behavioural classification of dreams as achromatic or chromatic.

Our principal hypotheses were framed to adjudicate between the two accounts outlined above:

1. *Language-causation prediction.* Functional connectivity between left inferior frontal and posterior temporal language regions and ventral occipitotemporal cortex during REM-rich sleep will be positively associated with vocabulary size and sentence length, and will explain variance in chromatic dream reports beyond that explained by age and maturational covariates.

2. *Shared-maturation prediction.* Associations between language-network connectivity and visual cortex activity will be substantially attenuated or eliminated after adjustment for white-matter integrity and sleep-EEG maturation indices, with the latter accounting for the relationship between linguistic measures and chromatic dreaming.

3. *Regional specificity.* Any language-related effect will be stronger in intermediate and ventral visual regions than in primary visual cortex.

By relating network-level measures to a behavioural phenomenon that has been independently replicated, we aim to move the question from the descriptive level at which it has rested since 2019 to a mechanistic one. We describe the participants, acquisition parameters, and analysis pipeline in Section 2, report results in Section 3, and consider their implications for models of how language and perceptual systems co-develop in Section 4.

---

## References (selected)

Desrochers, C., et al. (2019). Emergence of chromatic dream imagery in early childhood and its relation to language development. *Nature Neuroscience*.

Hellqvist, T., et al. (2022). Replication of the developmental timing of colour in children's dreams across Scandinavian samples. Multi-site study.

Horikawa, T., Tamaki, M., Miyawaki, Y., & Kamitani, Y. (2013). Neural decoding of visual imagery during sleep. *Science, 340*, 639–642.

Pooled review (2024). Colour and language in early dreaming: a synthesis of behavioural evidence and mechanistic accounts. *Developmental Review*.

---

**SOCIETY FOR EARLY CHILDHOOD DEVELOPMENT PRACTITIONERS**
**Evidence at a Glance** | Fact Sheet No. 14 | January 2025

# Night Terrors, Dreams, and Colour: What the Evidence Says About Early Childhood Dreaming

**Author:** Liesel Ahlberg, MD, Developmental Pediatrics
**For:** Clinicians conducting well-child visits (ages 18 months to 5 years)

---

## Why this sheet

Parents of toddlers and preschoolers often ask about nighttime behaviour: screaming, thrashing, apparent fear on waking, and "bad dreams." Clinicians increasingly also hear a related question: *what is my child actually seeing when they dream?* A consistent body of research now gives a clear answer about the visual character of early dreams, and it is useful for framing reassuring, accurate conversations.

## Key point

**Children dream in black and white until roughly age 3 to 4. The transition to colour dreaming follows language development.**

## The evidence

**Desrochers et al. (2019).** The foundational study, published in *Nature Neuroscience*, was conducted at the Child Sleep Laboratory, Marlowe University, Montreal, by Celine Desrochers and colleagues. The team followed 164 children using structured, age-adapted dream reports, with picture-matching tasks for the youngest participants. Findings:

- Children under 3 reported dreams exclusively in black and white.
- Colour appeared in dreams at ages 3 to 4.
- By age 3.2 years, half of the children reported dreaming in colour.
- The timing of colour onset tracked **vocabulary size and mean sentence length**, more closely than it tracked chronological age alone.

**Hellqvist et al. (2022).** Tomas Hellqvist and colleagues studied about 200 children in Sweden and Denmark. Their independent sample replicated both the timing of the transition and the association with language measures, across two languages and two healthcare contexts.

**Pooled review (2024).** A pooled review in *Developmental Review* combined the available datasets and confirmed both findings: the age window for colour onset and the link to expressive language. The review identified the underlying mechanism as unresolved.

## Night terrors are a separate issue

Night terrors (sleep terrors) arise from partial arousal out of deep non-REM sleep, typically in the first third of the night. The child is not experiencing a dream, usually has no recall, and is not awake despite open eyes and distress. The colour findings above concern dreams, which are reported from REM-related sleep. Parents often conflate the two, so it helps to separate them explicitly.

## What the open question is

The effect itself is not in dispute. What remains open is **causal direction**. Possible accounts include:

1. Language growth enables richer, more reportable dream imagery, including colour.
2. Underlying visual-cognitive maturation drives both language and dream colour.
3. A reciprocal relationship between the two.

Current data cannot separate these. This uncertainty does not change what we can tell families.

---

### WHAT TO TELL PARENTS

- "Young children's dreams are mostly in black and white. Colour usually appears around ages 3 to 4, as language grows."
- "A child who talks about colourful dreams at 3 or 4 is developing typically. So is one who does not yet."
- "Night terrors are different from dreams. Your child isn't aware of them and won't remember them. They are usually outgrown."
- During a night terror: stay close, keep the child safe, avoid waking them, and keep the room calm.
- Consistent bedtimes and adequate sleep reduce night terror frequency.
- Refer if episodes are nightly, last over 30 minutes, involve injury, or occur with snoring or breathing pauses.

---

## Practice notes

- Do not use dream colour as a screening tool. It is a population-level pattern, not a diagnostic marker.
- Dream reports below age 3 depend heavily on language ability, so interpret them cautiously.
- Children with language delay may reach colour dreaming later. This reflects the language association, not a separate concern.

## References

1. Desrochers C, et al. Colour onset in early childhood dreaming and its relation to language development. *Nature Neuroscience.* 2019. Child Sleep Laboratory, Marlowe University, Montreal.
2. Hellqvist T, et al. Replication of dream colour onset and language associations in Swedish and Danish children. 2022.
3. Pooled review of early childhood dream colour and language. *Developmental Review.* 2024.

# The Grayscale Nights of Toddlerhood

**Your two-year-old's dreams are real, vivid, and entirely without colour. Here is what science now knows about why, and why the colours are coming.**

*By Bronwen Okonkwo*

It was a Tuesday, a little after six in the morning, and Mabel was standing in her crib with the blanket draped over one shoulder like a tiny senator. I had barely opened my eyes when she announced, with great seriousness: "Gray dog. Big gray dog. Mama, gray dog *chased*."

My daughter is two. Her vocabulary is a lively, unreliable thing, with about two hundred words on a good day, and "gray" was not one I knew she had. I asked her what the dog was doing. "Running," she said. "Gray running." Then she asked for toast, and the matter was closed.

I did not forget it, though. I've spent eleven years writing about children and sleep, and I had a vague memory of something I'd once skimmed in a research digest and filed away under *interesting, revisit*. That morning I revisited it. What I found changed how I think about Mabel's nights, and I suspect it will change yours.

## The study that started the conversation

In 2019, a team led by Celine Desrochers at the Child Sleep Laboratory at Marlowe University in Montreal published a paper in *Nature Neuroscience* that has since become one of the most cited pieces of work in early sleep research. Desrochers and her colleagues followed 164 children over several years, tracking their sleep with a combination of overnight monitoring, parent-kept dream diaries, and, as the children grew old enough, gentle morning interviews.

The finding was strikingly consistent. Before about age three, the children reported dreams, and showed the physiological and behavioural signs of dreaming, only in black and white. Colour arrived later, in a window between ages three and four. By the time the children in the study reached 3.2 years, half of them were dreaming in colour.

"We went in expecting a gradual, patchy shift," Desrochers has said of the work. "What we saw was a fairly clean threshold. The grayscale period is real, it is universal in the sample, and it ends on a surprisingly predictable schedule."

If you're wondering how anyone knows what a two-year-old dreams, you're in good company. I wondered, too. The researchers relied on a layered approach. Toddlers too young to describe dreams were observed for sleep-talk, startle patterns, and the characteristic movements of rapid-eye-movement sleep. They were then asked simple, structured questions on waking, such as whether the dream was "bright" or "gray," with picture cards for children who could point but not yet explain. Parents kept diaries of every spontaneous report, much like the one I now keep on my phone for Mabel.

## Language is the clock

The most surprising part of the Desrochers paper was not *when* colour arrived but *what it tracked*. The children's timing was not explained by age alone. It followed language development, specifically vocabulary size and average sentence length. Children whose speech grew richer sooner began dreaming in colour sooner. Children who were a little later talkers stayed in grayscale a little longer.

"That was the headline for me," says Dr. Sanjay Kapoor, a sleep researcher who studies early childhood and who had no role in the Marlowe work. "The link to language was strong and it was specific. It wasn't a vague developmental correlation. It was the *same* children, ordered the same way, on both measures."

Kapoor, whom I reached by phone on a rainy afternoon while Mabel napped, is unequivocal about how much weight the finding can bear. "I'd describe it as as solid as anything in early sleep science," he told me. "It has not been retracted, it has not been corrected, and, importantly, nobody has mounted a serious challenge to it. In a field where results get quietly walked back all the time, that matters."

## Then it was done again

A single study, however carefully done, is a starting point. What turned the grayscale finding into something researchers treat as settled was what happened next.

In 2022, a team led by Tomas Hellqvist at a Scandinavian child development centre repeated the experiment from scratch. Their sample was larger, about 200 children across Sweden and Denmark, and drawn from a different population with different languages, different childcare traditions, and different bedtime routines. If the Montreal result had been a quirk of one place or one kind of family, this was the test that would expose it.

It didn't. Hellqvist's group found the same timing: grayscale dreaming in the youngest children, colour emerging between three and four. They found the same language link, with vocabulary and sentence length predicting when colour arrived.

"We were prepared for a different answer," Hellqvist said in a statement when the paper appeared. "Replication is where tidy results often fall apart. This one held, and it held across two languages and two countries."

In 2024, a review in *Developmental Review* pooled the two datasets, more than 360 children in all. It confirmed the age window and confirmed the language link. Kapoor calls that review "the point where I stopped thinking of this as a promising finding and started thinking of it as a fact about how children develop."

## The one question still open

If the *what* and the *when* are settled, the *why* is not, and the scientists are refreshingly candid about it.

The 2024 review lays out the central puzzle plainly. Does language actually *cause* colour dreaming? Perhaps once a child has words for "red" and "blue" and enough grammar to string a scene together, the brain has the scaffolding to build coloured imagery during sleep. Or are the two developments, speech and coloured dreams, both products of something deeper: a wave of brain maturation that unlocks both at roughly the same time?

"Those are genuinely different pictures," Kapoor explains. "In the first, if you could somehow accelerate a child's language, you might accelerate the colour. In the second, language and colour are siblings, not parent and child. The data we have right now can't separate them."

I find that oddly comforting. We know *that* it happens, we know *when*, and we know it travels alongside a child learning to talk. The remaining mystery is a narrow and interesting one.

## What this means at 6 a.m.

When I told my husband about all this, he asked the question every parent asks: "Is it bad? Is she missing something?"

No. There is nothing to fix, and nothing is lacking. Grayscale dreaming is simply the stage Mabel is in, as surely as she is in the stage of putting everything in her mouth and insisting on the blue cup. Her dreams are real. A big gray dog chased her, and to her it was exactly as vivid as anything she has ever seen.

If anything, the research invites a gentler kind of attention. The toddler years are the ones in which we most often assume children have no inner life at night, because they can't tell us about it. The Marlowe and Scandinavian studies suggest otherwise: a child who says "gray dog" is giving us a small, precise report from a place we can't otherwise visit.

There is a small additional gift in the timing. If you have a two-year-old who wakes upset, it can help to know that the frightening dog, the dark, the shapes, are rendered in shades of gray, and that the dreams will soften and brighten as language blooms. Colour is coming. For most families, it arrives sometime in the third year and settles in by the fourth.

I'll be watching for it. I've already started a note in my phone: *Mabel, 2y1m: gray dog. Gray running.* When the first "green" or "yellow" shows up in a dream report, I intend to write it down in whatever colour of ink I can find.

---

## SIDEBAR: What Parents Can Do

*You can't steer a toddler's dreams, and there's no need to. But the research suggests a few easy, warm habits that fit right into the rhythm of your day.*

**1. Talk about dreams at breakfast.**
Make "Did you dream last night?" a normal, low-pressure question. Don't push. If your child says "gray dog," follow with open, simple prompts: "What was the dog doing? Was it big or little?" You're giving your child practice describing an experience that isn't in front of them, which is exactly the kind of language work that matters at this age.

**2. Name colours all day long.**
Because colour dreaming tracks language, the everyday vocabulary of colour is worth building. "Can you find the red sock?" "Your spoon is yellow." "The leaves are turning orange." Researchers don't yet know whether words *cause* the shift, so think of this as enrichment, not a race. It's pleasant, it's free, and it makes mornings and walks more fun.

**3. Read and talk in longer sentences.**
Sentence length was one of the two measures that tracked colour onset. You don't need to quiz your child. Simply narrate your day in full sentences, expand on what they say ("Yes, a big dog, a big dog running across the park"), and read books with a bit of story to them.

**4. Take the dream seriously, but keep the comfort practical.**
If your toddler wakes frightened, validate first: "That sounds scary. You're safe now." Then a cuddle, a drink of water, a dim light. There is no need to explain dreams or correct them. Reassurance matters more than analysis.

**5. Keep a dream diary.**
A line or two in a notebook or phone app is plenty. Note the date, your child's age, and their exact words. It's a keepsake, and it lets you spot the moment colour appears. Many parents are delighted by the first "blue."

**6. Don't compare timelines.**
Half the children in the Montreal study were dreaming in colour by 3.2 years, which means half were not. Late talkers tend to reach colour a little later, and that is just the pattern the research describes. A child who is still in grayscale at three is right on schedule.

---

*Bronwen Okonkwo is a staff writer at* Little Hours. *She lives with her husband and her daughter, Mabel, who would like it known that the dog was very large.*

**Little Acorns Early Learning Centre | Monthly Parent Newsletter**

**From the Playroom: Dreams, Colours and Little Voices**
*By Vivienne Dalton, Lead Teacher*

If you have joined us for circle time lately, you will know that our mornings have taken a surprising turn. Where we once talked about the weather and who brought a favourite toy, we now hear about dreams. "I dreamed a big dog was in my bed." "I flew on a bus." "There was a monster, but he was nice." Our two-, three- and four-year-olds are keen to tell us what happened while they slept, and we love listening.

Their stories got me wondering what these dreams actually look like to a small child. So I went reading, and I would like to share what I found.

**Dreaming in black and white**

Children at this age mostly dream in black and white. Colour tends to arrive in dreams somewhere around the third or fourth birthday. If your toddler describes a dream in great detail but never mentions a red balloon or a green frog, that is completely typical.

The best-known research on this comes from a 2019 study in *Nature Neuroscience*, led by Celine Desrochers at the Child Sleep Laboratory at Marlowe University in Montreal. The team followed 164 children and, over time, gathered reports of their dreams. By the age of 3.2 years, about half of the children were reporting dreams in colour. What struck me most is that the shift was tied to language. Children with larger vocabularies and longer sentences were more likely to be dreaming in colour sooner.

A few years later, a Swedish-Danish team led by Tomas Hellqvist repeated the work in 2022 with about 200 children and found the same pattern. When two separate groups of researchers arrive at the same answer, we can feel confident about it.

**What this means at home**

None of this is cause for worry, and there is nothing you need to "fix." But because the link to language is so clear, there are some lovely, low-effort things you can do:

- **Ask about dreams over breakfast.** Keep it light: "Did you have a dream last night? Who was in it?" Don't push if your child doesn't feel like talking. Even a one-word answer is practice.
- **Invite more detail.** Try "What did it look like?" or "Was it big or small?" Children stretch their sentences when someone is genuinely curious.
- **Sprinkle colour words through your day.** "Let's find the yellow cup." "Your jumper is bright blue today." Colour words are easy to weave into getting dressed, cooking and walking to the park.
- **Read picture books with strong colours.** Pause and point. "What colour is the fox's tail?" Then see whether your child can tell you.
- **Draw the dream.** After a dream story, offer crayons and let your child draw it. Colour choices often lead to more talking.
- **Treat scary dreams gently.** Listen, reassure, and name the feeling ("That sounds scary, and you were brave to tell me"). Talking it through helps children feel safe.

**What we are doing at Little Acorns**

In the Acorn and Oak rooms, we have started a "Dream Corner" with soft cushions, a basket of coloured pencils and a few picture books about sleep. Children who want to share a dream can do so, then draw it if they wish. We are not testing anyone. We simply want every child to feel that their stories and words matter.

We have also added a colour-word game to circle time, where we pass around a mystery bag and describe what we find ("It's soft and orange!"). The children adore it, and the vocabulary growth has been wonderful to watch.

**One last thought**

Childhood goes by quickly, and these early conversations are precious. A few minutes of talk about a funny dream, even a black-and-white one, builds language, closeness and confidence all at once.

If your child has told you a particularly memorable dream, please share it with us at pickup. We would love to hear it, and so would the circle-time crowd.

Warmly,
Vivienne Dalton
Lead Teacher, Little Acorns Early Learning Centre

Air Weapons: The Little Little UAV Killer

January 21, 2020: The U.S. Air Force recently successfully tested the APKWS II (Advanced Precision Kill Weapons System) laser-guided missile fired from an F-16 fighter and shooting down a small UAV. The F-16 was using a targeting pod, which can spot and identify small flying objects and enable the pilot to launch an AGR-20A, as the APKWS used on jets is called, to hit a small, slow-moving target operating at low altitude. This means the AGR-20A can also be used against cruise missiles as well as UAVs of all sizes. The AGR-20A is currently most often used by slower-moving aircraft like helicopters and AC-130 gunships but was recently certified to operate from jet fighters. AGR-20A costs a third of what the larger Hellfire laser-guided missile does and more APKWS can be carried.

Missiles like APKWS have been around for over two decades and are basically 70mm laser-guided rockets. They were developed by taking a 13.6 kg (30 pound) 70mm unguided rocket and adding a laser seeker and moveable fins for guidance. These missiles have a 2.7 kg (six pound) warhead, and a range of about six kilometers when fired from the air. Laser designators on an aircraft, or with troops on the ground, are pointed at the target so the laser seeker in the front of the guided rocket can home in on the reflected laser light. The laser seeker can actually see reflected laser light out to 14 kilometers but the rocket motor in most 70mm laser-guided rockets is only effective at between five and ten kilometers.

The 2.75 inch (70mm) rockets were developed during World War II, as an air-to-air weapon for use against heavy bomber formations. The Germans had developed a similar and very successful weapon (the R4M). Since neither the Japanese nor the Germans had many heavy bombers the U.S. 70mm rocket was switched to air-to-ground use. Actually, the 70mm rocket was retained for air-to-air use into the 1950s, but it was never successful in that role until laser guidance was added.

The 70mm rocket became popular in the 1960s when it was discovered that the weapon worked very well when launched from multiple (7 or 19 tube) launchers mounted on helicopters. The 108-138m cm (42-55 inch) long rockets could be fired singly or in salvoes and gave helicopter pilots some airborne artillery for supporting troops on the ground. There are many variations in terms of warheads and rocket motors. Some versions could go over 10 kilometers.

Since the 1990s several firms have figured out how to turn 70mm unguided rockets into laser-guided missiles. Most were designed to use the existing the Hellfire missile fire control system. Several successful designs entered service by 2010. The APKWS began in 2002 when an American firm tried and initially failed making it work. British firm BAE took over and got it to working by 2007 and partnered with the American firm to sell it. APKWS, like its competitors, was built to be compatible with existing laser designators, and aircraft equipped to use Hellfire missiles. For helicopters, APKWS could also be adapted to use 7 or 19 tube launchers long employed for the unguided rockets. The chief advantage of all these 70mm missiles is that they are one fourth the weight of a Hellfire and  a third of the cost. That means AH-64s burn less fuel carrying them, and APKWS is as effective as a Hellfire in, for example, destroying the hundreds of small armed boats Iran plans to use in any war with the Arab states on the west coast of the Persian Gulf. But there are already many similar weapons available for this and few nations want to add what they consider a redundant weapon system. Swarms of cruise missiles and explosive equipped UAVs are another matter and in late 2019 Iran used such a swarm against Saudi oil facilities.

Despite the lack of demand, the 70mm missiles eventually found some customers. Back in 2010, the U.S. Marine Corps purchased fifty APKWS II kits for testing. That was followed by an order for kits to convert some of the 100,000 marine 70mm unguided rockets to laser-guided ones. In 2013 the marines made their third purchase, for over 20,000 newly manufactured APKWS II missiles. This was the first large purchase of 70mm guided missiles after a decade of sales efforts by several manufacturers. The marines arm their AH-1W helicopter gunships with the guided 70mm rockets and in 2012 marine AH-1Ws within a year had fired over a hundred APKWS II in Afghanistan and none of them missed.

APKWS was adapted for use from a number of helicopters as well as fixed-wing aircraft like the A-10, F-16, AV-8B, CN-235 gunship and A-29. APKWS has been exported to Iraq, Lebanon and Jordan and was used in 2017-18 in the fight against ISIL (Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant) in Iraq. Few fixed-wing aircraft can use Hellfire (only the British version of Hellfire, called Brimstone, has been adapted to use on fast-moving jets). American jet fighters have demonstrated that using APKWS is effective but current U.S. Air Force doctrine is to keep jet fighters at higher (above 6,000 meters) altitude to avoid most anti-aircraft fire. The A-10 was designed for low altitude operations and is an exception. The F-16 is expected to fill in if no A-10s are available for a close support mission. The navy and marines have allowed all fighter jets to get low when close air support of ground forces demands it.

There are now several guided versions of the 70mm air-to-surface and surface-to-surface versions. Developing a guided 70mm rocket took so long because the manufacturers underestimated the technical difficulties of getting the laser seeker and flight control mechanisms into that small a package, at a weight and price the customer could afford. The price of the new 70mm missile is now about $30,000 each. This is typical for these weapons and about a third less than a smart bomb and less than a third of what a Hellfire missile costs.

The guided 70mm rocket is used against targets that don't require a larger (49 kg/108 pound), and more expensive (over $100,000), Hellfire missile but still needs some targeting precision. In tests, the APKWS hit within a meter (a few feet) of the aiming point, about what other 70mm missiles are capable of. The 70mm missile makes an excellent weapon for UAVs, especially since you can carry more of them. The launcher for carrying these missiles is designed to replace the one for Hellfire but can carry four missiles instead of one. On jets, an AGR-20A launcher holds three of the missiles in place of one larger bomb or missile.

Orders for 70mm guided missiles were hard to obtain at first because the Hellfire was doing the job and there just wasn't a big demand for a smaller missile. There was another competition because several smaller missiles had recently been introduced and one of them, the Griffin, is being used over Pakistan and Afghanistan on American UAV as well as fixed-wing gunships (like the AC-130). The smaller Griffin is an alternative to the Hellfire II because it weighs only 16 kg (35 pounds) with a 5.9 kg (13 pound) warhead. Griffin has pop-out wings, allowing it to glide, and thus has a longer range (15 kilometers) than Hellfire (8,000 meters). UAVs can carry more of the smaller missiles, typically two of them in place of one Hellfire. The APKWS was found to be superior to the Griffin because, like Hellfire, it was fast and usually took no more than five seconds to reach the target.

In late 2019 the U.S. Department of Defense placed its first mass production order for AGR-20A. The manufacturer (BAE) received a $2.7 billion order to fill demand through 2025 from American (army, marines and air force) as well as a growing number of foreign customers which currently includes Britain, Iraq, Lebanon, Netherlands, Jordan, Afghanistan, Tunisia, Philippines and Australia. This order also includes kits for upgrading unguided 70mm (2.75 inch) rockets with a guidance system that turns them into AGR-20As. So far the AGR-20A has hit its intended target 90 percent of the time. Potential Persian Gulf customers like Saudi Arabia and the UAE (United Arab Emirates) already have jets equipped with targeting pods and now have an effective defense against Iranian UAV/cruise missile swarms. Israel is also now a potential user because they are facing enemies (Hezbollah, Hamas and Iran in Syria) who are using more small explosives carrying UAVs and the AGR-20A would be a less expensive way of dealing with these small target

**Q: My son is 2 and tells me about dreams. What are they like?**
*— Dalia Shah*

Dear Dalia,

What a gift, a two-year-old who reports from the night shift! I hear versions of this question often, usually from parents who are half charmed and half puzzled by a toddler announcing, over breakfast, "Dog. Big dog. Dark."

Here is what we know. At two, your son's dreams are most likely simple and in black and white. Think of a single animal, a familiar face, or a short scene with very little plot. They tend to be still, like a picture in a book, rather than the sprawling adventures you and I might have. If he says "doggy" and "night" and little else, that is probably a fair summary of the whole production.

Colour arrives later, usually between ages three and four. The most important work on this comes from Celine Desrochers and her colleagues at the Child Sleep Laboratory at Marlowe University in Montreal. Their 2019 study in *Nature Neuroscience* followed 164 children. By an average age of 3.2 years, half of them were describing dreams in colour. What I find lovely is that the shift tracked language. Children with larger vocabularies and longer sentences were the ones who reported colour sooner. Dreaming seems to grow up alongside talking.

Science works best when others check it, and this finding has held up. In 2022, Tomas Hellqvist and his team repeated the work with about 200 children across Sweden and Denmark and saw the same pattern. A 2024 pooled review in *Developmental Review* then brought the studies together and reached the same conclusion. When a result survives that many looks, we feel comfortable telling parents about it plainly.

Now for the anecdote, because I can't help myself. A few winters ago I looked after a little girl, just turned three, who was recovering from a long hospital stay. One morning she told her mother, quite seriously, "My dream was grey. Today my dream was red." Her mother laughed and wrote it on the whiteboard by the bed. Two days later, the dream was "red and a boat." I have never forgotten the pride in her voice. She had been given a new word for her nights.

A few suggestions for you at home:

- **Ask gently.** "What did you see?" works better than "What happened?"
- **Repeat his words back.** It helps build the vocabulary that seems to travel with dreaming.
- **Don't worry about scary dreams.** Short, simple fright is normal at this age. A cuddle and a night light go a long way.
- **Enjoy it.** These black-and-white dispatches won't last, and you'll miss them.

Thank you for writing, Dalia. Give your son a high five from the Glenmore team, and let me know when his dreams turn to colour.

Warmly,
*Hamish*

**Q: Do babies and toddlers dream in colour?**

**A:** Not at first! Very young children dream in black and white. Colour dreams usually begin when a child is about 3 or 4 years old.

**How do we know?**

Scientists can't peek inside a sleeping toddler's dream. But they can wake children gently, or ask them in the morning, and listen to what they say. Dr. Celine Desrochers did this at the Child Sleep Laboratory at Marlowe University in Montreal, Canada. She and her team studied 164 children. When the results were published in 2019 in a science journal called *Nature Neuroscience*, they showed something surprising.

Colour began to appear in children's dreams between ages 3 and 4. By age 3.2, which means three years and about two months, half the children were dreaming in colour.

**What else did she notice?**

Colour dreams seemed to arrive just as children were learning more words and building longer sentences. A child who could say "The big red dog ran home" was more likely to report a colourful dream than a child who could only say "Dog run."

**Did anyone else find the same thing?**

Yes! In 2022, a team of scientists in Sweden and Denmark, led by Dr. Tomas Hellqvist, studied about 200 children and found the same pattern. Then, in 2024, a review in the journal *Developmental Review* combined all the results and agreed. When different scientists in different countries find the same answer, we can feel more sure that it's true.

**What are scientists still asking?**

Here is the big puzzle. Does learning language *cause* colour dreams? Perhaps having words for "green" and "yellow" helps the brain build colour pictures during sleep. Or perhaps the brain is simply growing in two ways at the same time, one for talking and one for dreaming, with neither one causing the other. Nobody knows yet. Maybe one day you will help find out!

---

**TRY IT!**

Ask a grown-up you know: *"What is the earliest dream you can remember?"* Was it in colour? Was it scary, silly or strange? Most people can't remember dreams from before age 3 or 4, so you may find their earliest dreams all start around the same time. Write down what they tell you.

**THE SLEEP & DEVELOPMENT BULLETIN**
Newsletter of the Society for Developmental Sleep Research
Spring 2026 · Volume 31, Issue 1

## ROUNDTABLE

### What Would Settle the Mechanism Question?

*Three researchers set out the study each believes would best explain why children's dreams move from black and white to colour. Moderated by Odette Gunawardena. Written exchange, edited for length.*

---

**Odette Gunawardena (moderator):** Thank you all for agreeing to do this in writing. Dispensing with a live panel has the advantage that everyone can check their numbers before committing to them.

Let me begin with what nobody at this table disputes. Children dream in black and white until about age three to four, and colour then enters their dream reports. The finding rests on three pieces of work.

The first is the 2019 study in *Nature Neuroscience* led by Celine Desrochers at Marlowe University in Montreal. It followed 164 children with structured morning interviews and picture-matching tasks, and it established the basic developmental curve.

The second is Tomas Hellqvist's 2022 replication, with about 200 children in Sweden and Denmark. It used different interviewers, a different language environment and a revised response card, and it recovered the same curve.

The third is the 2024 pooled analysis in *Developmental Review*, which combined both datasets. Colour appears in dream reports between ages three and four. Half of the children report colour by 3.2 years. Earlier colour is associated with larger vocabulary and longer sentences.

The open question is mechanism. Does colour in dreams follow language development, or do both follow something else, such as cortical maturation? I asked each of you for the single study that would settle it. Ezra, you first.

---

**Ezra Vance:** I'd run an intervention. The pooled data give us a correlation between colour onset and language measures, and correlations cannot tell us which way the arrow points. So I would change the language environment and see whether the dream curve moves.

The design would be a randomised trial with children aged 24 to 30 months, before the typical transition. One arm would receive a structured shared-reading and conversation programme designed to raise vocabulary. The control arm would receive an attention-matched programme on motor play. Parents would complete the same morning dream-report protocol that Desrochers used, and interviewers would be blind to arm.

If language drives the transition, the language arm should reach the 3.2-year halfway point earlier. If colour onset is unaffected while vocabulary rises, the language account is in trouble. I'd want about 300 children to detect a shift of a couple of months.

The weakness is that vocabulary programmes produce modest gains, so a null result would be ambiguous. I'd accept that. A positive result would be hard to explain away.

---

**Mehmet Oduya:** I'd take a different route, because I worry that a spoken-language intervention conflates language with exposure to speech. My proposal is to study deaf children acquiring a sign language.

Deaf children of deaf, signing parents acquire language on roughly the same schedule as hearing children, but through a different modality. If the colour transition tracks language development itself, these children should show it on the same timetable. If it tracks auditory or speech-specific processes, they should diverge.

The more informative contrast is within the deaf population. Deaf children of hearing parents often have delayed access to any accessible language. Comparing them with native signers would give us a natural experiment on language delay with no intervention needed. A delayed-language group whose colour onset is also delayed would be strong evidence for the language account.

The challenges are sample size and measurement. We would need sign-language-fluent interviewers, and dream reports from signing toddlers must be elicited in a way that does not lean on spoken vocabulary. We would also need to compare against vocabulary checklists adapted for sign.

---

**Giulia Moretti:** I'd go below the behaviour. Both proposals use the same outcome, a parent's report of what the child says about a dream, and that outcome is itself a language product. If we are asking whether language drives the transition, using a language-based measure risks circularity.

I would follow children longitudinally from age two to five with repeated sleep reports and imaging of maturation. Structural and diffusion MRI, acquired during natural sleep or with the child resting quietly, every six months, would track visual association cortex and the white-matter tracts connecting it to temporal and frontal language regions. Sleep reports would be collected in dense bursts, say two weeks of daily interviews around each scan.

The analysis would ask whether tract maturation or cortical thickness change in visual regions precedes colour onset, whether language growth precedes it, or whether both follow a common timetable. With enough time points we could test lead-lag relationships directly, which a single correlation cannot do.

I accept this is the costliest of the three. Scanning toddlers is difficult and attrition will be high. But it is the only design that observes the candidate mechanisms rather than inferring them.

---

**Gunawardena:** Thank you. Celine, Tomas, you have both lived with these data. Does any of this change how you read your own results?

---

**Celine Desrochers:** It sharpens the question, which is what a good proposal should do. I'd note that in our 2019 sample, the vocabulary association survived adjustment for parental education and age, which makes a pure socioeconomic explanation unlikely. It does not tell us about direction.

I like Mehmet's design most as a first step, because it is feasible quickly and the contrast is clean. A group with delayed language access and a matched group without is exactly what the correlational data cannot give us. Ezra's trial would be a strong second step. I'd run Giulia's imaging study in parallel, because the neural account and the language account are not rivals in any simple way. Maturation could be what permits both.

My one caution on the intervention is timing. If the transition is gated by maturation, a language boost delivered at 24 months may simply arrive too early to matter, and we would learn less than we hope.

---

**Tomas Hellqvist:** I agree with most of that. From the replication I'd add a practical point. Our Scandinavian sample showed a slightly earlier median than the Montreal one, though within the margin of error, and the 2024 pooling treated site as a random effect. Any new study should be planned across several sites and languages from the start, so that we can separate language-specific effects from general developmental timing.

I'd also press for a shared reporting protocol across all three proposals. If the intervention study, the sign-language study and the imaging study all used the same morning interview and the same picture-matching card, their results could be combined in a single analysis. That is worth more than any one of them alone.

On Giulia's point about circularity, I think she is right, and it is the strongest argument for including a non-verbal element, such as a picture-choice response that does not require the child to produce words.

---

**Gunawardena:** Let me try to draw this together. There is agreement that the descriptive finding is secure and that the mechanism is the live question. There is also agreement on a sequence: the signing comparison first, because it is quickest, then the intervention trial and the imaging study. The shared protocol Tomas describes would let the three be pooled. The main disagreement is about how much weight to give a language-based outcome measure, and Giulia's objection means any future design should include a non-verbal response option.

I'd welcome letters from members with experience in sign-language assessment or paediatric sleep imaging. The Society's small-grants committee has indicated interest in a pilot of the shared protocol, and details of the next call will appear in the summer issue.

*Odette Gunawardena chairs the Society's Methods Working Group. Ezra Vance, Mehmet Oduya and Giulia Moretti contributed in a personal capacity. Correspondence to the editors of the Bulletin.*

# What Your Toddler's Dreams Say About Their Language

*By Noor Hamid, speech-language pathologist*

Last spring, a mother in my clinic told me something her two-and-a-half-year-old had said at breakfast. "I saw the dog. Big dog. Dog was *red*." She laughed, assuming it was a toddler's mix-up. But I stopped writing my notes. In my line of work, that sentence is a small window onto something quite remarkable.

I'm a speech-language pathologist, and I spend my days watching how children's words grow. One of the most surprising things I've learned in recent years has nothing to do with flashcards or story time. It's about what happens when your child is asleep.

## The colour of early dreams

For a long time, nobody knew what very young children dreamed about, or what their dreams looked like. Toddlers can't tell us much, and their reports are famously unreliable. That changed with a landmark 2019 paper in *Nature Neuroscience* by Dr. Celine Desrochers and her colleagues at the Child Sleep Laboratory at Marlowe University in Montreal.

The team followed 164 children using structured morning interviews. Picture cards and simple colour-matching tasks helped the youngest children show what they had seen, even when they couldn't describe it. The pattern was strikingly clear. Children younger than about three dreamed only in black and white. Colour began to appear between ages three and four. By around 3.2 years, half of the children were reporting dreams in colour.

What made the finding so important for people like me was what the colour tracked. It didn't line up neatly with age alone. It followed **vocabulary size and sentence length**. Children with larger vocabularies and longer, more complex sentences were the ones whose dreams had moved into colour, regardless of whether they were a few months older or younger than their peers.

## Has it held up?

It has. Science is right to be cautious about a single study, and the field responded the way it should. In 2022, Dr. Tomas Hellqvist's team repeated the work with about 200 children across Sweden and Denmark. Different country, different languages, different families, and the same developmental sequence emerged: black-and-white dreams first, colour arriving as language expanded.

In 2024, a pooled review in *Developmental Review* brought the evidence together and confirmed the pattern across the studies. This is now a well-established finding in child development, and I treat it as a foundation in my own practice.

## Does language cause colour dreaming?

This is where the real debate lives, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I skipped it. The research tells us that colour dreaming and language growth move together. It doesn't yet tell us *why*.

One view holds that language gives children the mental tools to label, sort and hold onto colour, so that words like "red" and "yellow" help build the colourful dream world. Another view says that neither causes the other. Instead, both may be riding on the same wave of brain maturation, the rapid development of memory, attention and representation that happens in the toddler years. Researchers are actively working on this, and I expect we'll learn more over the next several years.

For parents, the practical message doesn't depend on settling the question. Rich language and healthy development go hand in hand, and colour words are a wonderful, joyful place to build.

## Building vocabulary with colour words

Here are the strategies I share with families every week.

**1. Narrate colours during ordinary routines.** "You're wearing your blue socks. Let's put them in the green basket." Keep it casual. Toddlers learn most from language that's attached to what they're already doing.

**2. Pair the colour with the noun, then expand.** If your child says "ball," respond with "Yes, a red ball! A big red ball!" You've confirmed their word and added two more, without any pressure to repeat.

**3. Offer choices.** "Do you want the yellow cup or the purple cup?" Choices invite your child to say the colour word themselves, and they make the answer matter.

**4. Sort and match.** Colourful blocks, laundry, pasta shapes, or buttons are perfect. "Can you find another green one?" builds vocabulary and early categorising skills together.

**5. Read colour-rich books, and linger.** Don't rush through pages. Pause, point, and ask, "What colour is the bird's wing?" Then wait. Waiting is one of the most powerful tools in my kit.

**6. Make sentences longer, a little at a time.** Since sentence length is part of this story, stretch your child's phrases gently. If they say "red dog," you might say, "The red dog is running fast." Aim for just one step beyond where they are.

**7. Talk about yesterday.** Ask about the day's colours at bedtime: "What was the brightest thing you saw today?" Remembering and recounting build the kind of language that supports both memory and storytelling.

**8. Welcome the mistakes.** A purple banana or a red dog is a child experimenting, not failing. Reply warmly with the conventional word ("It looks like a yellow banana to me!") and move on.

## A note on expectations

Please don't treat any of this as a checklist for your child's dreams. You can't see inside your toddler's sleeping mind, and you don't need to. Children develop at different paces, and a two-year-old who doesn't yet use colour words isn't "behind" simply because of one milestone. If you have concerns about your child's speech or language, talk to your paediatrician or a speech-language pathologist. Early support makes a real difference.

What I love about this research is how it reminds us that language isn't only something children use. It seems to shape how they experience their inner world. Every time you name the colour of a leaf, a spoon or a sky, you're giving your child more than a word.

Sweet dreams, and happy talking.

*Noor Hamid is a speech-language pathologist who works with toddlers and preschoolers and their families. She writes about early communication, play and the everyday moments that build language.*
